one_liner: LLVM/MLIR ahead-of-time and JIT compiler for a TypeScript subset; no published speed comparison against Node/V8.
what_it_does: tslang compiles .ts files through its own MLIR 'ts' dialect to LLVM, emitting native executables, shared libraries, object files or wasm32 modules, or running them in-process with an LLJIT-based JIT that caches per-module object files in a __jit folder. Programs start at main() and use the project's own default library for JavaScript built-ins (print, arrays, strings, fetch via libcurl) instead of a JS engine, so it is a different toolchain, not a Node replacement. It also ships tsbindgen, which turns C headers into tslang declarations for calling C (and extern "C" wrappers of C++) directly.
how_it_is_fast: Static ahead-of-time compilation: TypeScript with its type annotations is lowered to typed ops in the project's own MLIR dialect (TypeScriptOps.td), with explicit integer types such as s32/i32 alongside number, then optimized by LLVM (--opt --opt_level=3), so there is no interpreter, inline cache or JIT warm-up. Memory is managed by the Boehm conservative collector by default, or by compiler-inserted reference counting (-mm=rc) or no freeing at all (-mm=none). No measurement in the repo shows that this beats V8; the only numbers are peak working set across the three memory models.
when_to_use: You want a single native binary (or a .dll/.so callable from C/C++) from TypeScript source with no Node, V8 or Bun on the target machine.
Embedding TypeScript-written logic in a C/C++ host via shared libraries and tsbindgen-generated C bindings, on Windows x64/x86, Linux x64 or Android (arm64-v8a, x86_64 cross-built from Windows).

Small memory footprint matters more than throughput: -mm=rc keeps a ray tracer at 4.1 MB peak working set versus 5.8 MB under Boehm GC, and a hello-world is 145 KB under -mm=rc versus 335 KB under -mm=gc (project's own figures).
Experimenting with TypeScript to wasm32 output without a JS engine inside the module (you supply the host imports yourself, as the README's run.html loader does).
when_not_to_use: You need a proven speedup over Node/V8: none is published, and the project's own reference-counting design doc says throughput is not the argument for its memory models.

Existing Node or npm code: Node APIs and npm packages are not available, the language subset has its own semantics (strict null checks, compile-time typing, main() entry), and the default library is the only source of JS built-ins.

Production use: releases are tagged v0.0-pre-alpha (latest v0.0-pre-alpha90), and basic-semantics bugs were fixed only days ago (#509 an empty string was truthy in conditions, #498 for await ran its body as concurrent tasks and lost writes, #456/#457 throws inside try not caught, #513 a mismatched object literal was silently not assigned).
Data with back-references under -mm=rc: parent links, doubly linked lists and closures capturing their owner are never freed; counts are non-atomic, so -mm=rc is single-threaded.
Building from source on a constrained machine: the README asks for about 50 GB of free disk for the LLVM/MLIR build (prebuilt release packages avoid this).

integration.form: compiler toolchain (prebuilt tslang release packages, or built from source with CMake/Ninja); output is native exe, dll/so, object file or wasm32
integration.dependencies: LLVM/MLIR 22.1.8 (to build the compiler), Boehm GC (for -mm=gc), the tslang async runtime library and the separate TypeScriptCompilerDefaultLib default library; libcurl for fetch() (stubbed on Android, where fetch() throws)
integration.min_toolchain: Windows: Visual Studio 2026; Linux: gcc or clang with cmake, ninja-build and libtinfo-dev (README tested on Ubuntu 20.04 and 22.04)
integration.platforms: Windows x64 and x86, Linux x64, Android arm64-v8a and x86_64 (API 29+, cross-compiled from a Windows host), wasm32-unknown-unknown (-mm=none); the JIT is host-only
integration.thread_safety: Not documented for user code. -mm=rc uses non-atomic counts and is single-threaded per docs/memory-models.md; -mm=gc shared libraries had thread races in Boehm registration fixed on 2026-10-06 (#522, #523).

gotchas: No benchmark against Node, V8, Deno or any other runtime exists in README, docs/memory-models.md or tslang/docs/reference-counting-evaluation.md; every number compares the compiler's own -mm=gc/-mm=rc/-mm=none modes (peak working set, --opt --opt_level=3, no hardware stated). The design doc's section 9.28 shows the same ray tracer at 129.5 MB under -mm=rc before the discarded-temporaries fix, so the 4.1 MB headline depends on very recent ownership work.

Windows -mm=gc: if an executable and a tslang shared library each link the static gc.lib, each gets its own collector and one frees objects the other still holds; the symptom is plausible wrong values, not a crash. Current tslang links gc.dll automatically for --emit=dll and refuses old statically linked libraries, but hand-linked builds must use the shared gc.lib.
Mixing modules built with different -mm values compiles with only a warning, and objects crossing between them leak.

0 open issues, and the 25 most recent were all filed and closed by the maintainer within the last week; the README badge says the project is developed with Claude Code. Expect fast churn and little outside bug reporting.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over katsu, LLRT or lo when you want TypeScript compiled to a standalone native or wasm binary or a C-callable shared library with no JS engine at all; pick those siblings when you need measured wins over Node (katsu's cold start, LLRT's Lambda cold start) or Node/npm compatibility.
verified_claims_summary: No speed claim was verified: the repo only reports peak working set of its own builds (ray tracer 256x256: 5.8 MB gc, 4.1 MB rc, 114.5 MB none; 512x512: 5.5 / 4.1 / 445.0 MB; n-body 5.6 / 4.1 / 4.1 MB) at --opt --opt_level=3 with no hardware or OS stated, and no Node/V8 baseline was run.
status_note: Very active (last commit 2026-10-06, hundreds of commits) and MIT-licensed, but still pre-alpha with a fast-moving language subset; usable for experiments and C/C++ embedding, not as a measured faster alternative to Node.
